observations.content:
Summary: PEP 703 proposes making the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional in CPython by adding a build configuration flag `--disable-gil` to the configure script, allowing CPython to run without the GIL and with necessary changes to make the interpreter thread-safe. The GIL will remain the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads. The PEP is final and was accepted by the steering council, with the implementation affecting installers, build-backends, and build orchestration tooling. The sources do not provide a definitive answer on the exact release date of the initial implementation.

# What is PEP 703?

by Tim Hopper ·  Markdown

PEP 703: Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython is the proposal that makes a no-GIL CPython build real. It adds a build configuration that removes the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), the mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, producing the free-threaded Python interpreter.

[2] PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython | peps.python.org
    https://peps.python.org/pep-0703
    The global interpreter lock will remain the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads. A new build configuration flag, `--disable-gil` will be added to the configure script that will build CPython with support for running without the global interpreter lock.

When built with `--disable-gil`, CPython will define the `Py_GIL_DISABLED` macro in Python/patchlevel.h. The ABI tag will include the letter “t” (for “threading”). [...] See PEP 1 for how to propose changes.

## Abstract

CPython’s global interpreter lock (“GIL”) prevents multiple threads from executing Python code at the same time. The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs from Python efficiently. This PEP proposes adding a build configuration (`--disable-gil`) to CPython to let it run Python code without the global interpreter lock and with the necessary changes needed to make the interpreter thread-safe.

Summary: PEP 703 proposes adding a build configuration to CPython to run Python code without the global interpreter lock (GIL) and make the interpreter thread-safe. PEP 779 outlines three phases of development for removing the GIL, with the free-threaded build becoming officially supported but still optional in phase II. PEP 805 discusses the challenges of parallel execution without the GIL, emphasizing the need for safe parallel Python to avoid race conditions and dangerous bugs. The sources do not provide a definitive timeline for the completion of these phases or the exact status beyond phase II.

[1] PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython | peps.python.org
    https://peps.python.org/pep-0703
    See PEP 1 for how to propose changes.

## Abstract

CPython’s global interpreter lock (“GIL”) prevents multiple threads from executing Python code at the same time. The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs from Python efficiently. This PEP proposes adding a build configuration (`--disable-gil`) to CPython to let it run Python code without the global interpreter lock and with the necessary changes needed to make the interpreter thread-safe.

## Motivation [...] This PEP proposes a new API `PyDict_FetchItem` which behaves like `PyDict_GetItem`, but returns a new reference instead of a borrowed reference. As described in Borrowed References, some uses of borrowed references that were safe when running with the GIL are unsafe when running without the GIL and need to be replaced by functions like `PyDict_FetchItem` that return new references. [...] The GIL is a CPython implementation detail that limits multithreaded parallelism, so it might seem unintuitive to think of it as a usability issue. However, library authors frequently care a great deal about performance and will design APIs that support working around the GIL. These workaround frequently lead to APIs that are more difficult to use. Consequently, users of these APIs may experience the GIL as a usability issue and not just a performance issue.

This PEP changes `PyMem_Malloc()`: it now always calls `malloc()` rather than `PyObject_Malloc()`. The “GIL must be held” restriction could therefore be removed from `PyMem_Malloc()`. Summary: PEP 703 proposes adding a build configuration to CPython to run Python code without the global interpreter lock (GIL), allowing for true parallel execution of Python bytecode across multiple CPU cores. The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs efficiently. The PEP was finalized in October 2023 and is part of Python 3.13, with an experimental "free-threaded" build introduced in Python 3.13 as part of this PEP. The GIL will remain the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads, but a new build configuration flag, --without-gil, will enable a GIL-less interpreter.

# What is PEP 703?

by Tim Hopper ·  Markdown

PEP 703: Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython is the proposal that makes a no-GIL CPython build real. It adds a build configuration that removes the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), the mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, producing the free-threaded Python interpreter.

    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_interpreter_lock
    In Python 3.13, an experimental "free-threaded" build of CPython was introduced as part of PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython. This build allows developers to compile Python without the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), enabling true parallel execution of Python bytecode across multiple CPU cores. The feature is still experimental but represents a major step toward improved concurrency in future Python releases.

In implementations with a GIL, there is always one GIL for each interpreter process "Process (computing)").

Summary: PEP 703 proposes adding a build configuration (`--disable-gil`) to CPython to run Python code without the global interpreter lock (GIL) and with necessary changes to make the interpreter thread-safe. The PEP suggests using biased reference counting and switching from a generational to a non-generational garbage collector for the no-GIL build. The steering council aims to eventually have a single build of CPython, either without the GIL if it works out or reverting to the with-GIL version if it does not. The proposal is not definitive about the end state for the no-GIL build.

    https://peps.python.org/pep-0703
    Removing the GIL requires changes to CPython’s reference counting implementation to make it thread-safe. Furthermore, it needs to have low execution overhead and allow for efficient scaling with multiple threads. This PEP proposes a combination of three techniques to address these constraints. The first is a switch from plain non-atomic reference counting to biased reference counting, which is a thread-safe reference counting technique with lower execution overhead than plain atomic reference [...] This PEP proposes switching from a generational cyclic garbage collector to a non-generational collector (when CPython is built without the GIL). That is equivalent to only having one generation (the “old” generation). There are two reasons for this proposed change. [...] See PEP 1 for how to propose changes.
